content: Apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 (ASK-1) is a critical component of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade. In humans, ASK-1 is also referred to as mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase 5 (MAP3K5). The MAPK signaling pathways consist of a series of kinases, including MAPK or extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), MAPK kinase (MKK or MEK), and MAPK kinase kinase (MAPKKK or MEKK). Within this cascade, MAPKKK/MEKK phosphorylates and activates its downstream kinase, MAPK kinase/MEK, which subsequently activates MAPK. These kinases are highly conserved across species, with homologs identified in yeast, Drosophila, and mammalian cells. Phosphorylation of the ASK-1 protein can trigger apoptosis or other cellular responses, depending on the specific cell type. Northern blot analysis has demonstrated that ASK-1 transcripts are abundantly expressed in human heart and pancreas tissues. The ASK-1 protein (MAP3K5) is capable of phosphorylating and activating MKK4 (also known as SERK1 or MAPKK4) in vitro. Additionally, ASK-1 activates c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), also referred to as stress-activated protein kinase (SAPK), during transient expression in COS and 293 cells. However, ASK-1 does not activate MAPK/ERK. In its inactive state, ASK-1 is bound to reduced thioredoxin (Trx). Upon oxidation by reactive oxygen species (ROS), Trx dissociates from ASK-1. This dissociation allows ASK-1, which exists as a homo-oligomer, to undergo autophosphorylation and become an active MAP kinase kinase kinase. Structurally, ASK-1 is composed of 1,374 amino acids and contains all 11 kinase subdomains.
